### Supporting basis
A composite B-tree index on (customer_id, created_at) is superior for this specific workload. PostgreSQL can efficiently satisfy the query by using the first column to locate the customer and the second to filter the date range, enabling an Index Only Scan or rapid Index Scan. Separate indexes fail here because PostgreSQL typically cannot merge two B-tree indexes for complex range queries efficiently; it would likely perform a sequential scan or use only the customer_id index, requiring costly row lookups for every date check. With 10 million rows and even distribution, about 10% of customers (10,000) are accessed daily. Each customer averages ~27 rows per day. The composite index minimizes I/O by directly accessing only the relevant seven-day slice. Separate indexes create maintenance overhead and inefficient execution plans for range joins. Empirical benchmarks on similar datasets show composite indexes reduce query latency by 5-10x compared to single-column indexes for this pattern, as they avoid unnecessary table heap accesses and leverage index order for range filtering.

### Recommendation
Choose the single composite B-tree index on (customer_id, created_at). This structure perfectly matches the query's SELECT * pattern, allowing PostgreSQL to quickly identify the customer and then iterate through the sorted dates within that customer's partition. Since the query retrieves all columns, an Index Only Scan is unlikely unless the row size is small, but the index still drastically reduces random I/O by providing sorted, sequential access to the necessary rows. Separate indexes offer no benefit for this specific range filter and may degrade performance during concurrent writes due to higher index update overhead. Ensure your random_page_cost is tuned if running on SSDs to favor index scans. This strategy ensures consistent, low-latency reads for the 10,000 daily active customers while maintaining manageable storage overhead. The composite index is the standard best practice for "lookup by entity, filter by time" patterns in relational databases.<|im_end|>
